'''Jerry Lee Rice''' (born October 13, 1962)<ref name="Pro-Football-Ref-1" /> is an American former professional [[American football|football]] [[wide receiver]] who played for 20 seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He won three [[Super Bowl]] titles with the [[San Francisco 49ers]] before two shorter stints at the end of his career with the [[Oakland Raiders]] and [[Seattle Seahawks]]. For his accomplishments and numerous records, Rice is widely regarded as the greatest wide receiver of all time and one of the greatest players in NFL history.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.espn.com/blog/nfcwest/post/_/id/13874/the-case-for-rice-as-the-greatest-ever |title=The case for Rice as the greatest ever |last=Sando |first=Mike |date=February 4, 2010 |archive-date=December 1, 2017 |url-status=dead }}</ref> His biography on the official [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]] website names him "the most prolific wide receiver in NFL history with staggering career totals".<ref name="pfhof">{{Cite web |title=Jerry Rice |url=https://www.profootballhof.com/players/jerry-rice/ |access-date=June 3, 2022 |website=Pro Football Hall of Fame Official Site |language=en |archive-date=May 19, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220519235825/https://www.profootballhof.com/players/jerry-rice |url-status=live }}</ref> In 1999, ''[[Sporting |title=Sporting News Top 100 Football Players |page=3D |work=Democrat and Chronicle |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/4376402/sporting_news_top_100_football_players/ |url-status=live |access-date=February 27, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181116023025/https://www.newspapers.com/clip/4376402/sporting_news_top_100_football_players/ |archive-date=November 16, 2018 |via=Newspapers.com}}</ref> In 2010, he was chosen by [[NFL Network]]'s [[NFL Films]] production ''[[The Top 100: NFL's Greatest Players]]'' as the greatest player in NFL history.<ref name="Barall-2010" />

Rice played [[college football]] for four seasons with the [[Mississippi Valley State Delta Devils football|Mississippi Valley State Delta Devils]], setting several [[National Collegiate Athletic Association]] (NCAA) and team receiving records, including becoming the all-time leader in NCAA receiving touchdowns. He joined the 49ers after being selected with the 16th overall pick of the [[1985 NFL draft]]. After a modest rookie season, Rice emerged in the following season as one of the best receivers in the league, leading the NFL in receiving yards and touchdowns, a feat he achieved six times. In 1987, Rice set the record for most receiving touchdowns in a season, with 22, in a twelve-game strike-shortened season. He won back-to-back championships in [[Super Bowl XXIII|1988]] and [[Super Bowl XXIV|1989]], and was the MVP of the former championship. Rice developed connections with quarterbacks [[Joe Montana]] and [[Steve Young]] that are viewed as among the best in NFL history, helping him lead the league in both receiving yards and touchdowns six times, and in receptions twice.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Santorsa |first=Tony |date=December 7, 2011 |title=NFL History: Top 50 QB-WR Tandems of All-Time |url=https://bleacherreport.com/articles/972343-top-50-qb-wr-tandems-in-nfl-history |access-date=June 3, 2022 |website=Bleacher Report |language=en |archive-date=June 3, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220603183939/https://bleacherreport.com/articles/972343-top-50-qb-wr-tandems-in-nfl-history |url-status=live }}</ref>

Going into the 1990s, Rice won a third Super Bowl in [[Super Bowl XXIX|1994]], and a second Offensive Player of the Year Award. After recovering from a knee injury and his play regressing, San Francisco released him in June 2001, where the Raiders would sign him to a four-year deal. He continued to start for the team, and helped lead them to an appearance in [[Super Bowl XXXVII]], where they were defeated by the [[2002 Tampa Bay Buccaneers season|Tampa Bay Buccaneers]], affecting Rice's previously unblemished Super Bowl record. Midway through 2004, the Raiders traded him to the Seahawks, where he spent his final season.<ref>{{Cite web |date=October 19, 2004 |title=Raiders agree: Rice to Seattle |url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=1904779 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180626191129/http://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=1904779 |archive-date=June 26, 2018 |access-date=August 13, 2022 |website=[[ESPN.com]] |language=en |agency=[[Associated Press]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Cour |first=Jim |date=October 20, 2004 |title=Rice's trade to Seahawks reunites star wide receiver with Holmgren |url=https://www.spokesman.com/stories/2004/oct/20/rices-trade-to-seahawks-reunites-star-wide/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220814011946/https://www.spokesman.com/stories/2004/oct/20/rices-trade-to-seahawks-reunites-star-wide/ |archive-date=August 14, 2022 |access-date=August 13, 2022 |website=The Spokesman-Review |agency=[[Associated Press]]}}</ref> He briefly signed with the Broncos, retiring shortly before the start of the 2005 regular season.

Rice is the career leader in most major statistical categories for wide receivers,<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.nfl.com/history/randf/records/indiv/receiving |title=Individual Records: Receiving |website=NFL.com |access-date=April 24, 2011 |archive-date=October 15, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181015205829/http://www.nfl.com/history/randf/records/indiv/receiving |url-status=live }}</ref> including [[Reception (American football)|reception]]s, receiving [[touchdown]]s, receiving yards, scrimmage yards, and total touchdowns, holding the postseason records for these statistics, and once held the single-season records for yards and touchdowns. He scored more points than any other non-[[Placekicker|kicker]] in NFL history with 1,256.<ref name="PointsScoredPFR">{{Cite web |title=NFL Points Scored Career Leaders |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/leaders/scoring_career.htm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181125132126/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/leaders/scoring_career.htm |archive-date=November 25, 2018 |access-date=October 29, 2018 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref> Rice was selected to the [[Pro Bowl]] 13 times (1986–1996, 1998, 2002) and named All-Pro twelve times in his 20 NFL seasons, including ten First-team All-Pros, tied for the most by any player. Rice was inducted into the [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]] in 2010 and the [[College Football Hall of Fame]] in 2006. Rice was inducted into the [[Mississippi Sports Hall of Fame]] in 2007, and in the same year was inducted into the [[Bay Area Sports Hall of Fame]]. The NFL honored him as a member of the [[NFL 1980s All-Decade Team]] and the [[NFL 1990s All-Decade Team]], as well as both the [[NFL 75th Anniversary All-Time Team]] and [[NFL 100th Anniversary All-Time Team]].

== Early life ==
Jerry Lee Rice Sr. was born on October 13, 1962, in [[Starkville, Mississippi]],<ref name=pfhof/> and grew up in [[Crawford, Mississippi]], the sixth of eight children.{{Sfn|Sterngass|2008|p=13}} Crawford was a small town, having only 600 residents.<ref name="Dickey-1993">{{Cite book |last=Dickey |first=Glenn |url=https://archive.org/details/sportsgreatjerry00dick/page/18/mode/2up?q=father&view=theater |title=Sports Great Jerry Rice |publisher=[[Enslow Publishers]] |year=1993 |isbn=9780894904196 |location=New Jersey |pages=13, 17, 18, 23 |language=English |url-access=registration}}</ref> Rice's father, Joe, was a brick mason who built houses by hand, while holding other jobs to provide for the family.{{Sfn|Rice & Curtis|2007|p=5}} Joe was described by Rice as "a tough man" and held him and his siblings to a strict lifestyle.<ref name="NFL Network-2014">{{Cite episode |title=Jerry Rice |series=A Football Life |series-link=A Football Life |network=NFL Network |date=January 28, 2014}}</ref> Eddie B., Rice's mother, raised Rice while Joe was working, and after Rice left cleaned the houses of wealthy families.{{Sfn|Rice & Curtis|2007|p=31}} Rice and his brothers often worked with their father building houses, catching bricks on top of scaffolds to make sure his father had bricks to lay.<ref name="NFL Network-2014"/> He did not see bricklaying as being his future saying that "it taught me the meaning of hard work."<ref name="Grabowski-2002">{{Cite book |last=Grabowski |first=John |url=https://archive.org/details/sanfrancisco49er0000grab_z7r8/page/84/mode/2up?q=rice |title=The San Francisco 49ers |publisher=[[Lucent Books]] |year=2002 |isbn=1560069473 |location=San Diego, CA |pages=84, 85, 86, 87 |language=English |url-access=registration}}</ref> The Rice family struggled financially, with Rice sometimes not having many pairs of clothing or having a "hearty meal on the table".{{Sfn|Rice & Curtis|2007|p=7}} Providing for his family, he and his brothers picked corn, cotton, carrots, and hay.{{Sfn|Rice & Curtis|2007|p=8}} Rice asserted that he was shy as a child and did not have many friends.{{Sfn|Rice & Curtis|2007|p=10}}

Rice attended [[B. L. Moor High School]] in [[Oktoc, Mississippi]]. Although he played mock games of [[basketball]] and football, Rice did not initially play sports for his high school.{{Sfn|Rice & Curtis|2007|pp=10, 11}} He enjoyed playing [[sandlot football]] and watching football on television. His mother forbade him to join the school's football team in his freshman year, as she thought that football was "too rough" for Rice.{{Sfn|Sterngass|2008|p=18}} During Rice's sophomore year, the school's assistant principal caught him skipping class with a friend, causing him to panic and sprint away. After Rice fled, the principal was impressed with his speed, and informed the school's football coach, Charles Davis, who offered Rice a place on the team.{{Sfn|Sterngass|2008|p=18}} Initially unhappy about this, Rice's mother relented after realizing that "the more I fought it, the more determined he was, so I gave it up."{{Sfn|Sterngass|2008|p=18}}

Rice played multiple positions in high school, including [[running back]], [[defensive back]] and [[tight end]], but the position he was most skilled at was [[wide receiver]].<ref name="Dickey-1993" /> During the offseason before his junior year, he trained for the team by running the several miles back to his home as he did not have a ride.{{Sfn|Rice & Curtis|2007|p=15}} Rice had a breakout junior season, primarily playing wide receiver and defensive back.{{Sfn|Rice & Curtis|2007|p=15}} In his senior year, Rice was a Mississippi All-State selection at wide receiver.

Due to the small size of Moor, few of his statistics were officially recorded.<ref name="Grabowski-2002" /> According to sports journalist Glenn Dickey, Rice caught 50 receptions and 30 touchdowns as a senior, helping to lead the team to a {{abbr|17–2|17 wins, 2 losses}} record over his final two seasons.{{Sfn|Sterngass|2008|p=18}}<ref name="Dickey-1993" /> He and Moor's starting quarterback, Willie Gillespie, were very dependable, enough for them to be nicknamed [[Johnny Unitas]] and [[Raymond Berry]].<ref name="Dickey-1993" /> In addition to football, Rice also played [[basketball]] as a [[Forward (basketball)|forward]] and participated on the [[track and field]] team, competing in the [[high jump]].{{Sfn|Sterngass|2008|p=19}}

Rice received over 40 contacts from [[NCAA Division I|NCAA Division I-A]] schools; his preference was to attend [[Mississippi State University]], but they did not offer him an [[athletic scholarship]].{{Sfn|Sterngass|2008|p=23}} He was drawn to [[Mississippi Valley State Delta Devils football|Mississippi Valley State]], in part because the school's coach, [[Archie Cooley]], ran a pass-heavy offense—enough that Cooley was nicknamed "The Gunslinger."<ref>{{Cite web |last=Jenks |first=Jayson |date=December 1, 2020 |title=How the no-huddle offense evolved via tweakers, tinkerers — and The Gunslinger |url=https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/2190190/2020/12/01/how-the-no-huddle-offense-evolved-via-tweakers-tinkerers-and-the-gunslinger/ |access-date=March 14, 2022 |website=The Athletic |language=en |archive-date=March 15, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220315011931/https://theathletic.com/2190190/2020/12/01/how-the-no-huddle-offense-evolved-via-tweakers-tinkerers-and-the-gunslinger/ |url-status=live }}</ref> After Cooley watched Rice play in person and after he visited the school's campus, Rice committed to playing at Mississippi Valley State.{{Sfn|Rice & Curtis|2007|p=20-21}}

==College career==
Rice attended [[Mississippi Valley State University]] from 1981 to 1984.<ref>{{Cite web |date=August 20, 2015 |title=FWAA Names MVSU's Jerry Rice To 75th Anniversary All-America Team |url=https://hbcusports.com/2015/08/20/fwaa-names-mvsus-jerry-rice-to-75th-anniversary-all-america-team/ |access-date=April 15, 2023 |website=HBCU Sports |language=en-US |archive-date=April 15, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230415232331/https://hbcusports.com/2015/08/20/fwaa-names-mvsus-jerry-rice-to-75th-anniversary-all-america-team/ |url-status=live }}</ref> When Rice arrived at Mississippi Valley State, he attended summer school and freshman orientation before the regular season. Two of his former teammates from B.L. Moor were there as well, but both left before the start of training camp.{{Sfn|Rice & Curtis|2007|p=22–23}} Rice studied receiving techniques from [[Gloster Richardson]], stating: "I soaked up everything I could."{{Sfn|Sterngass|2008|p=27}}
[[File:Jerry Rice - Mississippi Valley - November 1983 (cropped).jpg|thumb|170px|Rice with the [[Mississippi Valley State Delta Devils]] in 1983]]
In 1981, Rice's freshman season, he caught 30 passes for 428 yards and two touchdowns.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Pierron |first=Jeff |date=December 16, 1984 |title=Rice ready to reap football dividends |page=14 |work=[[The Greenwood Commonwealth]] |url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/249366415/?terms=%22jerry%20rice%22%20%22428%22&match=1 |access-date=June 11, 2022 |via=Newspapers.com |archive-date=June 12, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220612015731/https://www.newspapers.com/image/249366415/?terms=%22jerry%20rice%22%20%22428%22&match=1 |url-status=live }}</ref> In 1982, his sophomore year, Rice played his first season with freshman [[quarterback]] [[Willie Totten]].<ref name="Gardner">{{cite news |last1=Gardner |first1=Sam |date=October 21, 2014 |title=Jerry Rice, Valley lit up scoreboards 30 years ago |work=Fox Sports |url=http://www.foxsports.com/college-football/story/jerry-rice-mississippi-valley-lit-up-scoreboards-30-years-ago-102114 |url-status=dead |access-date=June 12, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160523024740/http://www.foxsports.com/college-football/story/jerry-rice-mississippi-valley-lit-up-scoreboards-30-years-ago-102114 |archive-date=May 23, 2016}}</ref> They became friends and practiced into the evening.{{Sfn|Sterngass|2008|p=27–28}} Under the direction of Cooley, Mississippi Valley State ran an "unusual" offense, playing four wide receivers who tended to line up on one side of the field.{{Sfn|Sterngass|2008|p=28}} Rice caught 66 passes for 1,133 yards and seven touchdowns.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Potter |first=Jerry |date=November 16, 1982 |title=Jackson State, Valley, dominate All-SW AC selections |pages=2C |work=[[The Clarion-Ledger]] |url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/183591347/?terms=jerry%20rice%20%221%2C133%22&match=1 |access-date=June 5, 2022 |via=Newspapers.com |archive-date=June 5, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220605062321/https://www.newspapers.com/image/183591347/?terms=jerry%20rice%20%221,133%22&match=1 |url-status=live }}</ref> Together, Totten and Rice became known as "The Satellite Express."{{Sfn|Sterngass|2008|p=27–28}} Success on the field did not put any money in his pocket, and many times he relied on friends for food, stating that the food given to him at Mississippi Valley "were not enough for a growing man".{{Sfn|Rice & Curtis|2007|p=24}} Rice had a record-setting 1983 campaign, including NCAA marks for receptions (102) and receiving yards (1,450). He was named a first-team Division I-AA [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]].<ref name="Nissenson-1983">{{cite news|last1=Nissenson|first1=Herschel|title=Idaho Star Leads AP Team|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/9992991/idaho_star_leads_ap_team/|access-date=April 2, 2017|work=Daily Sitka Sentinel|agency=[[Associated Press]]|date=December 28, 1983|page=5|via=Newspapers.com|archive-date=April 3, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170403111427/https://www.newspapers.com/clip/9992991/idaho_star_leads_ap_team/|url-status=live}}</ref> He set a single-game NCAA record with 24 receptions against [[Southern University]]. He acquired the nickname "World," because of his ability to seemingly catch anything thrown near him.<ref name="Gardner" />

After an August practice experiment, Cooley had Totten call all the plays at the [[Hurry-up offense|line of scrimmage without a huddle]], resulting in even more staggering offensive numbers.{{Sfn|Sterngass|2008|p=28}} Rice caught 17 receptions for 199 yards against Southern, 17 receptions for 294 yards, and five receiving touchdowns against [[Kentucky State Thorobreds football|Kentucky State]], and 15 for 285 yards against [[Jackson State University|Jackson State]].{{Sfn|Sterngass|2008|p=30}}<ref>{{Cite news |date=November 2, 1984 |title=NCAA Division I-AA Individual Game Highs for 1984 season |pages=31 |work=Democrat and Chronicle |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/97814691/ncaa-division-i-aa-individual-game/ |access-date=March 17, 2022 |via=Newspapers.com |archive-date=March 17, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220317201811/https://www.newspapers.com/clip/97814691/ncaa-division-i-aa-individual-game/ |url-status=live }}</ref> During the game against Kentucky State, Rice caught twelve passes and scored three touchdowns in a single quarter.{{Sfn|Sterngass|2008|p=30}} As a senior in 1984, he surpassed his own Division I-AA records for receiving yards (1,845), and receptions (112); his 27 touchdown receptions in the 1984 season set the NCAA record for every division.<ref name="Gardner" /> The 1984 Delta Devils averaged more than 60 points per game.{{Sfn|Sterngass|2008|p=29}} Rice was named to the Division I-AA All-American team and finished ninth in [[Heisman Trophy]] balloting in 1984.<ref name="Services-1984">{{Cite news |date=December 27, 1984 |title=Knox wins UPI award |pages=2B |work=[[The Miami Herald]] |url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/631254363/?terms=jerry%20rice%20mississippi%20valley%20state&match=1 |access-date=March 17, 2022 |via=Newspapers.com |archive-date=March 17, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220317201758/https://www.newspapers.com/image/631254363/?terms=jerry%20rice%20mississippi%20valley%20state&match=1 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=1984 Heisman Trophy Voting |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/awards/heisman-1984.html |access-date=March 15, 2022 |website=College Football at Sports-Reference.com |language=en |archive-date=December 12, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211212172803/https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/awards/heisman-1984.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

===San Francisco 49ers (1985–2000)===
Rice's record-breaking season at Mississippi Valley State caught the attention of NFL scouts. === Retirement ===
On September 5, 2005, Rice announced his retirement after 20 seasons.<ref>{{cite news | first1=Gina | last1=Pace | url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/football-legend-jerry-rice-retires/ | publisher=CBS News | title=Football Legend Jerry Rice Retires | date=September 5, 2005 | access-date=April 2, 2017 | archive-date=November 11, 2013 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131111182651/http://www.cbsnews.com/stories/2005/09/05/archive/main816606.shtml | url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="NFL Network-2014"/> Because he never played for Denver outside of the preseason, Rice was only allowed his guaranteed money for a grand total of $25,000.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Saunders |first=Patrick |date=May 25, 2005 |title=Star receiver Jerry Rice to join Broncos |url=https://www.denverpost.com/2005/05/25/star-receiver-jerry-rice-to-join-broncos/ |access-date=April 15, 2023 |website=The Denver Post |language=en-US |archive-date=April 15, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230415232603/https://www.denverpost.com/2005/05/25/star-receiver-jerry-rice-to-join-broncos/ |url-status=live }}</ref> In August 2006, the 49ers announced that Rice would sign a contract with them, allowing him to retire as a member of the team where his NFL career began. On August 24, 2006, he officially retired as a 49er, signing a one-day contract for $1,985,806.49. The number represented the year Rice was drafted (1985), his No. 80, the year he retired (2006), and the 49ers (49). The figure was ceremonial, and Rice received no money.<ref>{{Cite news |date=August 24, 2006 |title=Rice signs one-day deal to retire as a 49er |work=USA Today |agency=[[Associated Press]] |url=http://usatoday30.usatoday.com/sports/football/nfl/niners/2006-08-24-rice-ceremony_x.htm |url-status=dead |access-date=August 3, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130813142115/http://usatoday30.usatoday.com/sports/football/nfl/niners/2006-08-24-rice-ceremony_x.htm |archive-date=August 13, 2013}}</ref> A halftime ceremony honored him during the 49ers' match-up with the Seattle Seahawks on November 19, 2006.<ref>{{cite news|title=Jerry Rice: One Retirement Isn't Enough|url=https://abcnews.go.com/Sports/story?id=2337394&page=1|access-date=April 2, 2017|publisher=ABC News|date=August 21, 2006|archive-date=April 3, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170403194722/http://abcnews.go.com/Sports/story?id=2337394&page=1|url-status=live}}</ref>

Rice is remembered as one of the best clutch players in football history, often making game-winning catches throughout his career. Rice also was noted as an effective blocking receiver.{{Sfn|O'Brien|2005|p=46}} Rice's "famous" catching ability, sometimes attributed to him having to catch bricks when working with his father during his childhood, led him to 1,549 career receptions, 117 ahead of the second-place Fitzgerald.<ref>{{Cite web |title=NFL Receptions Career Leaders |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/leaders/rec_career.htm |access-date=June 14, 2023 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref>{{Sfn|Sterngass|2008|p=16}}

Despite being keen about his public image early in his career, Rice is remembered for his work ethic and dedication.{{Sfn|Sterngass|2008|pp=90, 11, 15, 16}} He still cared extensively about his physical appearance, often tailoring his uniform and jersey, and combed his hair before putting on his helmet; his philosophy was: "If you look good, feel good, you'll play good", as described by Shawn Rogers, one of his friends.<ref name="NFL Network-2014"/> In his 20 NFL seasons, Rice missed only 17 regular season games, 14 of them in the 1997 season and the other three in the strike-shortened season of 1987; his 303 games are the most by an NFL wide receiver by a wide margin.{{Sfn|Sterngass|2008|p=119}} In addition to staying on the field, his work ethic showed in his dedication to conditioning and running precise routes, with coach [[Dennis Green]] calling him "the best route runner I've ever seen".{{Sfn|Sterngass|2008|p=8}} One of the best-known examples of his dedication and ethic was "The Hill," a steep hill in [[Edgewood County Park|Edgewood County Park & Natural Preserve]] which is {{convert|2.5|mi|km|0}} long. Rice sprinted across the hill every day during the offseason to improve his abilities.{{Sfn|Sterngass|2008|p=91}}

== Personal life ==
Rice married Jacqueline "Jackie" Bernice Mitchell on September 8, 1987. Jacqueline Rice filed for divorce in June 2007, which became final in late December 2009. They have three children, Jaqui Bonet (born 1987), [[Jerry Rice Jr.]] (born 1991), and Jada Symone (born 1996). Jerry Jr., who attended high school at [[Menlo School]] in [[Atherton, California]], graduated in 2009. He was a walk-on at [[UCLA Bruins football|UCLA]] and redshirted his first season.<ref name="Uclabruins.com-1991">{{Cite web |date=July 27, 1991 |title=Player Bio: Jerry Rice, Jr. – UCLA Official Athletic Site |url=http://www.uclabruins.com/sports/m-footbl/mtt/ricejr_jerry00.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110430100450/http://www.uclabruins.com/sports/m-footbl/mtt/ricejr_jerry00.html |archive-date=April 30, 2011 |access-date=April 24, 2011 |website=UCLA Bruins Athletics}}</ref><ref name="Paloaltoonline.com-2009">{{Cite web |date=March 26, 2009 |title=Menlo's Jerry Rice Jr. commits to UCLA |url=http://www.paloaltoonline.com/news/show_story.php?id=11754 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120320014225/http://www.paloaltoonline.com/news/show_story.php?id=11754 |archive-date=March 20, 2012 |access-date=September 8, 2012 |website=Palo Alto Online}}</ref> After three seasons and limited playing time, Jerry Jr. graduated from UCLA and transferred to [[University of Nevada, Las Vegas|UNLV]], and was eligible to play immediately.<ref name="Uclabruins.com-1991" /> He played wide receiver for the [[UNLV Rebels football|Rebels]] and participated in a 49ers local pro day before the [[2014 NFL draft]], but was not drafted.<ref name="ESPN-2014">{{Cite web |date=May 13, 2014 |title=Reports: Ravens invite Jerry Rice Jr. |url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/10925080/baltimore-ravens-invite-jerry-rice-jr-rookie-minicamp |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140517011847/http://espn.go.com/nfl/story/_/id/10925080/baltimore-ravens-invite-jerry-rice-jr-rookie-minicamp |archive-date=May 17, 2014 |access-date=May 14, 2014 |website=[[ESPN.com]]}}</ref> Jerry Rice has another son, [[Brenden Rice]], who played football for the [[University of Colorado Boulder]] for two years. On January 1, 2022, it was announced that Brenden was transferring to the [[University of Southern California]].<ref>{{Cite magazine |last=McCarty |first=Andrew |date=January 1, 2022 |title=Brenden Rice, Son Of NFL Legend Jerry Rice, Announces Transfer |url=https://thespun.com/college-football/brenden-rice-son-of-nfl-legend-jerry-rice-announces-transfer |access-date=January 1, 2022 |magazine=[[Sports Illustrated|The Spun]]}}</ref> As of October 21, 2019, Rice is married to Latisha Pelayo whom he had dated since 2008.<ref name="secondmar">{{Cite web |last=Kimble |first=Lindsey |date=October 21, 2019 |title=NFL Legend Jerry Rice Marries Latisha Pelayo in Napa Ceremony |url=https://people.com/sports/jerry-rice-marries-latisha-pelayo/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191106221328/https://people.com/sports/jerry-rice-marries-latisha-pelayo/ |archive-date=November 6, 2019 |access-date=November 6, 2019 |website=People.com}}</ref>

Rice is a [[Christianity|Christian]]. He said he grew up as a Christian and still has the same faith from his youth.<ref>{{cite web |title=Hall of Fame Special with Jerry Rice, Troy Polamalu and Isaac Bruce |url=https://faithonthefieldshow.com/hall-of-fame-special-with-jerry-rice-troy-polamalu-and-isaac-bruce/ |website=Faith On The Field |access-date=October 11, 2023}}</ref>
